lead: A receiver adds noise of its own, so the signal-to-noise ratio at its output is lower than at its input. Noise figure and noise temperature put that loss into one number. With them an engineer compares amplifiers, decides what goes first in a receiver chain, and predicts the SNR that reaches the demodulator. This chapter defines both, relates them, and combines stages in cascade with the Friis formula.
prereq: You need: thermal noise power kTB and noise bandwidth from Noise sources, white noise and AWGN, and decibels.

blocks.text: Feed an amplifier of power gain G from a matched source at the standard temperature T0 = 290 K. The input noise is kT0B. The output noise No is G kT0B (amplified input noise) plus Na, the noise the amplifier adds. The noise factor F compares the two SNRs:

blocks.where: F is a linear ratio with no unit; the second form follows because the signal is amplified by G as well; F = 1 + N<sub>a</sub>/(G kT<sub>0</sub>B).

blocks.text: F is at least 1, and a noiseless device has F = 1. The noise figure is the same quantity in decibels, NF = 10 log10 F: F = 2 is NF = 3.01 dB. Some syllabi use "noise figure" for both. Datasheets quote NF in dB; formulas need linear F, because noise powers add and gains multiply. T0 = 290 K (about 17 °C) is a fixed convention, not the room temperature of the day.

The equivalent noise temperature Te describes the added noise as if it came from an extra matched resistor at the input: the added noise power, referred to the input, is kTeB, and at the output it is G kTeB. Te is a bookkeeping temperature, not the physical temperature of the device. Putting Na = G kTeB into the formula for F gives

blocks.where: T<sub>e</sub> and T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K are in kelvin; F is linear.

blocks.text: F = 2 means T<sub>e</sub> = 290 K. Noise temperature suits very quiet devices: an LNA with NF = 1 dB has T<sub>e</sub> = 75 K, and a few kelvin are easier to compare than the second decimal of a dB value.

A lossy cable or attenuator with power loss L (input power over output power, L ≥ 1) has gain G = 1/L. At physical temperature T0 its noise factor equals its loss, F = L, so Te = (L − 1)T0. A 3 dB loss (L = 2) is F = 2 and Te = 290 K; a 6 dB loss (L = 3.981) is Te = 864.5 K.

A receiver is a chain of stages with linear gains G1, G2, … and noise factors F1, F2, …. Each stage's added noise, referred back to the chain input, is divided by the total gain in front of it. That gives the Friis formula, in two equivalent forms:

A large G<sub>1</sub> makes every later term small, so the first stage sets the noise of the whole chain. That is why a receiver puts a low-noise amplifier (LNA) with good gain first, and why loss in front of it is costly: a cable before the LNA has G<sub>1</sub> < 1, which multiplies every later term instead of dividing it.

items: Convert every NF to F = 10<sup>NF/10</sup> and every gain to G = 10<sup>G(dB)/10</sup>; a loss of L dB is F = 10<sup>L/10</sup> and G = 1/F.
Put the linear values into Friis, keeping at least four significant figures.
Convert back: NF = 10 log<sub>10</sub> F, or T<sub>e</sub> = (F − 1)T<sub>0</sub>.

blocks.text: The antenna delivers noise of its own, described by the antenna temperature Ta (sky and ground seen by the beam). The system noise temperature is Tsys = Ta + Te, and the noise power at the receiver input is kTsysB.

examples.question: A two-stage receiver has stage 1 with gain 20 dB and noise figure 3 dB, and stage 2 with gain 20 dB and noise figure 6 dB. Find the overall noise factor, noise figure and equivalent noise temperature (T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K).
steps: NF = 10 log<sub>10</sub> 2.025 = 3.06 dB, only 0.06 dB worse than stage 1 alone.

Check with the temperature form: T<sub>e1</sub> = 0.995 × 290 = 288.6 K and T<sub>e2</sub> = 2.981 × 290 = 864.5 K, so T<sub>e</sub> = 288.6 + 864.5/100 = 288.6 + 8.6 = 297.3 K. The gain of stage 2 does not enter: nothing follows it.

examples.question: A 1 MHz receiver chain has an antenna of temperature T<sub>a</sub> = 50 K, a cable with 2 dB loss at 290 K, an LNA (G = 20 dB, NF = 1 dB) and a mixer (G = 10 dB, NF = 8 dB). Find T<sub>e</sub>, NF, T<sub>sys</sub> and the input noise power (a) with the cable before the LNA, and (b) with the LNA moved to the antenna and the cable after it.
steps: Noise power kT<sub>sys</sub>B with B = 10<sup>6</sup> Hz: (a) 1.38×10<sup>−23</sup> × 363.0 × 10<sup>6</sup> = 5.01×10<sup>−15</sup> W (−113.0 dBm); (b) 2.09×10<sup>−15</sup> W (−116.8 dBm).

Moving the LNA ahead of the cable lowers the noise by 10 log<sub>10</sub>(363.0/151.2) = 3.8 dB, so the same signal arrives with 3.8 dB more SNR. In (a) the cable's 2 dB loss also divides the LNA's term by 0.631, raising it from 75.1 K to 119.0 K.
examples.answer: (a) T<sub>e</sub> = 313.0 K, NF = 3.18 dB, T<sub>sys</sub> = 363.0 K, −113.0 dBm. (b) T<sub>e</sub> = 101.2 K, NF = 1.30 dB, T<sub>sys</sub> = 151.2 K, −116.8 dBm: 3.8 dB better.

traps: Do not add noise figures in dB, and do not put dB values into Friis. Convert to linear F and G, apply the formula, then convert back.
T<sub>0</sub> is 290 K, not 300 K. Using 300 K shifts every T<sub>e</sub> and is a common marking error.
F is linear and NF is in dB. F cannot be below 1, so NF cannot be negative.
A lossy cable at T<sub>0</sub> has F = L and gain 1/L. Before the LNA it adds its own noise and also multiplies the later stages' terms by L.
The last stage's gain never appears in Friis. And T<sub>e</sub> is referred to the input: at the output the added noise is G kT<sub>e</sub>B.

quiz.q: Define noise factor and noise figure, and state the reference temperature.
quiz.a: Noise factor F = SNR<sub>in</sub>/SNR<sub>out</sub> (linear), measured with a matched source at T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K. Noise figure NF = 10 log<sub>10</sub> F in dB.

quiz.q: Why is the noise factor never less than 1?
quiz.a: The device amplifies the input signal and input noise by the same G and then adds noise of its own, so the output SNR can only fall. Hence SNR<sub>in</sub>/SNR<sub>out</sub> ≥ 1, with F = 1 only for a noiseless device.

quiz.q: An amplifier has F = 4. Find its noise figure and its equivalent noise temperature.
A 6 dB attenuator at 290 K sits before an amplifier. Find its noise factor, its gain and its noise temperature.
Two stages have F<sub>1</sub> = 1.5, G<sub>1</sub> = 20 dB and F<sub>2</sub> = 3, G<sub>2</sub> = 20 dB. Find the overall noise factor and say which stage matters more.
quiz.a: G<sub>1</sub> = 100, so F = 1.5 + (3 − 1)/100 = 1.52 (NF = 1.82 dB). Stage 1 dominates: stage 2 adds only 0.02 after division by G<sub>1</sub>.

quiz.q: Why must dB noise figures be converted to linear values before using Friis?
quiz.a: Friis adds noise powers referred to the input and divides them by linear power gains. A dB value is a logarithm; adding logarithms multiplies the ratios, which is not what the noise powers do.

quiz.q: Write the Friis formula for three stages in noise-factor and noise-temperature form.
quiz.a: F = F<sub>1</sub> + (F<sub>2</sub> − 1)/G<sub>1</sub> + (F<sub>3</sub> − 1)/(G<sub>1</sub>G<sub>2</sub>); T<sub>e</sub> = T<sub>e1</sub> + T<sub>e2</sub>/G<sub>1</sub> + T<sub>e3</sub>/(G<sub>1</sub>G<sub>2</sub>), with linear gains.

beyond: Not for the exam. Noise figure is measured by the Y-factor method, comparing the output noise with a calibrated noise source on and off. Radio telescopes cool their first amplifier to cut its noise temperature. Receiver sensitivity is −174 dBm/Hz + 10 log<sub>10</sub>B + NF + the SNR the demodulator needs. Search for Y-factor method and receiver sensitivity.
